subsection: 2. Independence struggles in Indochina and the East Indies

notes.h: Background: colonial rule and the shock of the Japanese conquests
notes.b: Before 1941 France and the Netherlands ruled most of South-East Asia as colonies. To understand why that rule collapsed after 1945, you need to know what colonial rule was and what Japan did to its prestige.
points: Colonial rule means that a foreign state controls a territory and runs it for its own benefit. France ruled Indochina and the Netherlands ruled the East Indies, and the region mattered to both for products and markets such as rubber, tin and trade.

De-colonisation is the process by which colonies win independence from the imperial power. Here it was driven by nationalist movements, which had to fight or negotiate against European powers that wanted to return after 1945.

Japan's conquests of 1941–42 and its occupation shattered the image of European invincibility, because Asian peoples watched European armies and officials driven out. This is why nationalists could now believe that European rule could be ended.

The Cold War, the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, shaped the later struggle. After the communist victory in China (1949) and during the Korean War, the United States viewed Vietnam in Cold War terms, so it backed France against Ho.
notes.tip: Ordinary Level document questions on the French Union and the Vietnam war ask you to identify the French Union, say what the United States was doing and explain why the region mattered (rubber, tin, trade). Read the document for the answer rather than relying on memory.

notes.h: French Indochina: formation and government
notes.b: France did not rule its Indochinese possessions as a single colony. It built a federation in which different areas had different legal status, which is why the status of Cochinchina became a problem in 1946.
points: French Indochina was formed as a federation in 1887 from Tonkin, Annam, Cochinchina and Cambodia (Tonkin, Annam and Cochinchina being the three regions of Vietnam), and Laos was added in 1893.
The French ruled through a colonial administration headed by a governor-general, with the capital of the federation at Hanoi, so real power lay with French officials rather than local rulers.
Cochinchina, in the south, was a direct colony run by French officials. Tonkin, Annam and Cambodia were protectorates, meaning territories that kept a local ruler but were controlled by France.
The Vietnamese emperor was kept in place as a figurehead (a ruler with a title but no real power) at Hue.
Do not confuse the Indochinese Federation of 1887, which was Indochina's own unit, with the French Union of 1946, which covered France and its overseas lands.
notes.tip: Examiners expect you to keep the 1887 Indochinese Federation and the 1946 French Union apart, because they are two different bodies with different dates.

notes.h: The Japanese occupation, the Viet Minh and the August Revolution, 1940–1945
notes.b: Japan's arrival in 1940 began to loosen French control, and its coup in 1945 removed it. Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh used the gap to take power in August 1945.
points: Japanese troops entered northern Indochina in September 1940 with the agreement of Vichy France (the wartime French government that cooperated with Germany), so the French administration was allowed to carry on for a time under Japanese pressure.
Japan overthrew the French administration in a coup on 9 March 1945 and took full control, which ended French rule and left a power vacuum.

The Viet Minh (League for the Independence of Vietnam) was founded in May 1941 under Ho Chi Minh. It was a front, an alliance of groups, combining communists and non-communist nationalists, so it could appeal to Vietnamese of many views. Vo Nguyen Giap led it in the field.

Its wartime fighting against the Japanese was small-scale guerrilla activity (hit-and-run raids), not a large campaign. In 1945 the OSS, the American wartime intelligence service, gave it some supplies and training.
A famine in northern Vietnam in 1944–45 killed many people. Estimates of deaths range from about 400,000 to about 2 million, so give the range rather than a single figure.

The Viet Minh seized power in Hanoi and other towns in August 1945, an event called the August Revolution. Emperor Bảo Đại abdicated on 25 August 1945, which removed the figurehead emperor the French had kept at Hue.
notes.tip: Keep the three Vietnamese communist bodies apart: the Indochinese Communist Party (1930), the Viet Minh (1941, a front) and the Lao Dong Party (the ruling party of the North after 1954). The wartime Viet Minh fought a small guerrilla war, not a large campaign.

notes.h: Vietnam: independence declared and the return of France, 1945–1946
notes.b: With the Japanese gone, Ho Chi Minh declared independence at once. But the Allies divided the country between their own forces, and France used the opening to return.
points: On 2 September 1945 in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. He opened with words from the American Declaration of Independence (and also cited the French Declaration of the Rights of Man), turning the ideals of the Western powers against colonial rule.

After Japan's surrender, Chinese Nationalist troops occupied the north (to the 16th parallel) and British forces the south. British troops helped the French regain control in Saigon in September 1945, so France had a foothold in the south.

In the Franco-Vietnamese agreement of 6 March 1946, France recognised the Democratic Republic as a free state within the Indochinese Federation and the French Union. The status of Cochinchina was left to a promised referendum, which never took place.
The French Union was created by the constitution of the Fourth Republic in 1946. It was a federation of France, its overseas departments and territories, and associated states.
The French Union fell short of independence because France kept control of defence and foreign policy. A ‘free state’ inside it could not run its own army or its relations with other countries.
notes.tip: When describing the 6 March 1946 agreement, name both the Indochinese Federation and the French Union, and say that the promised referendum on Cochinchina never took place.

notes.h: From talks to war, 1946
notes.b: Neither side trusted the March agreement. During 1946 talks in France failed, a bombardment hardened feeling, and fighting in Hanoi began a long war.
points: Ho Chi Minh went to France for the Fontainebleau conference in the summer of 1946 and signed a temporary agreement on 14 September 1946, but the talks failed to settle the main disagreements.
A French naval bombardment of Haiphong in November 1946 killed many civilians (no figure is agreed), which made war very likely.
Fighting broke out in Hanoi on 19 December 1946, which started the First Indochina War (1946–54) between France and the Viet Minh.
Ho Chi Minh wrote several letters and telegrams to President Truman in 1945–46 asking for American support. None was answered, so he approached the war without American help at this stage.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the First Indochina War (1946–54, against France) with the later American war in Vietnam.

notes.h: The war becomes a Cold War issue, 1949–1950
notes.b: France could not win by force alone, so it set up a Vietnamese alternative to Ho. At the same time the Cold War drew China and the United States into the conflict.
points: France set up the State of Vietnam under Bảo Đại in 1949 as an alternative to the Democratic Republic, and Western states recognised it.

Keep the names apart: the Democratic Republic of Vietnam was Ho's state in the North, while the State of Vietnam of 1949 was the French-backed one. The Republic of Vietnam of the South dates only from 1955.
China's communist government, in power from October 1949, supplied the Viet Minh with weapons and military advisers from 1950, which strengthened Ho's army.
By the early 1950s the United States paid for a large share of the French war effort, because it viewed the war as part of the struggle against communism.
Ho's government in the north was recognised by China and the Soviet Union, so the two sides in Vietnam now had powerful outside backers.
notes.tip: A strong answer treats the war as a Cold War issue: China aided Ho from 1950 while the United States paid much of France's cost.

notes.h: Dien Bien Phu, 1953–1954
notes.b: In 1953 the French tried to end the war with one decisive battle. At Dien Bien Phu the plan backfired and French hopes of victory ended.
points: General Henri Navarre, French commander from 1953, wanted a decisive battle, so he fortified the valley at Dien Bien Phu in north-west Vietnam, close to Laos, to draw the Viet Minh into a set-piece fight.
The siege ran from 13 March to 7 May 1954.

Vo Nguyen Giap hauled artillery up the hills surrounding the valley and supplied his army over long routes by porters and bicycles, so the French garrison below was under heavy fire and could not be relieved.
The French garrison surrendered, and about 10,000 French Union troops (soldiers from France and its overseas lands) were captured.
The Indochina talks at Geneva opened on 8 May 1954, the day after the surrender.
notes.tip: Weak answers narrate Dien Bien Phu without saying why it ended the war. Link the surrender to the Geneva talks and the 1954 division of Vietnam.

notes.h: The Geneva Conference and Accords, 1954
notes.b: The French defeat made a settlement urgent. Geneva ended the French war but divided Vietnam, which set the stage for later conflict.
points: The Geneva Conference, which opened on 26 April 1954, covered both Korea and Indochina. Pierre Mendès France became French prime minister in June 1954 promising a settlement within a month, so France was now ready to negotiate.
The ceasefire agreements of July 1954, together known as the Geneva Accords, divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel and planned elections to unite the country in 1956.
The Accords also made Laos and Cambodia independent.
The United States did not sign the accords, which left it free to support a separate government in the South.
notes.tip: Say ‘July 1954’ for the ceasefire agreements rather than giving one exact date, and remember that the United States did not sign. Link the Accords to Dien Bien Phu and to the 1954 division.

notes.h: After Geneva: the South, the North and the end of French rule, 1954–1956
notes.b: The Accords did not bring unity. The division hardened, France left, and the United States took its place in the South.
points: The elections planned for 1956 were never held, because the South's government, backed by the United States, refused to hold them.
Ngô Đình Diem became premier of the South in 1954 and president in 1955 with United States backing.
French forces withdrew from the South by 1956, and the United States replaced France as the main outside power in South Vietnam.
In the North the Lao Dong (Workers') Party ran the state under Ho Chi Minh, with Soviet and Chinese aid.
Ho's land reform of 1953–56, which redistributed land from landlords to peasants, was violent, and the government publicly admitted errors in 1956.

notes.h: Laos and Cambodia, 1953–1954
notes.b: The other two parts of French Indochina took a different path from Vietnam. Both gained independence from France in 1953.
points: In Cambodia King Norodom Sihanouk's ‘royal crusade’, a campaign he led to press France for independence, helped win independence in 1953.
Laos also became independent in 1953, though within the French Union at first. Geneva in 1954 confirmed the independence of both Laos and Cambodia.
In Laos the communist Pathet Lao, allied to the Viet Minh, held areas in the north-east and fought the royal government after 1954.

notes.h: The Dutch East Indies: occupation and the proclamation of independence, 1942–1945
notes.b: The Japanese occupation ended Dutch control and allowed Indonesian nationalists to build organisations and armed forces. When Japan surrendered, they declared independence before the Dutch could return.
points: The Japanese occupation of 1942–45 ended Dutch rule. It drew heavily on Indonesian forced labourers, known as romusha, but it also put Indonesians in senior positions that they had never held under the Dutch.
The Japanese trained Indonesian forces, notably the PETA volunteer army set up in 1943, so Indonesians gained weapons and military skills that could later be used against the Dutch.
The Japanese allowed nationalists such as Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta to speak publicly, which gave them a platform to reach ordinary Indonesians.
On 1 June 1945 Sukarno gave a speech setting out the Pancasila, five principles on which an independent Indonesia would be based.
Sukarno and Hatta proclaimed Indonesian independence in Jakarta on 17 August 1945, two days after Japan announced its surrender. Sukarno became president and Hatta vice-president.
The Dutch refused to recognise the proclamation until the transfer of sovereignty in 1949, so independence had to be won against them.

Dutch forces returned with Allied support in late 1945. British and Indonesian forces fought at Surabaya in November 1945, and British forces withdrew in 1946, leaving the Dutch troops to face the Republic.
notes.tip: Keep the Pancasila speech (1 June 1945), the proclamation (17 August 1945) and the transfer of sovereignty (27 December 1949) as three separate dates.

notes.h: The Dutch war: Linggadjati to Renville, 1946–1948
notes.b: The Dutch were willing to talk but not to give up control. The agreements they signed were vague, and each led to new fighting.
points: The Linggadjati Agreement was initialled on 15 November 1946, with formal signing following in 1947. The Netherlands recognised the Republic's de facto authority (its authority in practice) over Java, Madura and Sumatra, but Dutch sovereignty was retained in the interim.

It also provided for a federal United States of Indonesia linked to the Netherlands in a union. The Dutch and the Republic then disagreed over what it meant, and the Dutch reinterpreted it in their own favour.
The first Dutch ‘police action’ (the Dutch name for a military offensive) began in July 1947 and occupied much of the Indonesian-held territory in Java and Sumatra.
The UN Security Council called for a ceasefire in August 1947 and set up a Good Offices Committee, so the dispute now became an international matter.
The Renville Agreement of January 1948 was signed aboard the US ship Renville and left Dutch forces holding large parts of Java and Sumatra.
notes.tip: The police actions (Dutch term, 1947 and 1948) are not the same as Konfrontasi (1963–66, against Malaysia). Name the event, the date and a consequence for each.

notes.h: Madiun, the second police action and international pressure, 1948–1949
notes.b: The Republic survived a crisis at home and a second Dutch attack. International reaction then turned against the Dutch.
points: In September 1948 the Republic's forces put down a communist rising at Madiun, which helped to win American sympathy for the Republic because it showed the Republic would fight communists.

The second police action of 19 December 1948 took Yogyakarta, the Republic's capital at the time, and imprisoned Sukarno and Hatta. A government in exile on Sumatra continued the resistance, so the capture did not end the war.

The UN Security Council demanded a ceasefire and the release of the leaders. Its resolutions of December 1948 and January 1949 also called for restoration of the Republic's government, but did not formally condemn the Dutch.

United States pressure on the Netherlands, which included the threat that Marshall Plan aid (the American programme of aid for rebuilding postwar Europe) could be affected, helped bring the Dutch to the negotiating table.
notes.tip: Strong answers show that diplomatic pressure from the UN and the United States mattered as much as fighting in bringing Indonesian independence.

notes.h: The transfer of sovereignty, 1949
notes.b: Under pressure, the Dutch finally negotiated. The settlement gave Indonesia independence but left some disputes open.
points: The Round Table Conference at The Hague (August–November 1949) settled the terms of independence.
Sovereignty was transferred on 27 December 1949 to the Republic of the United States of Indonesia.
Indonesia agreed to take over about 4.3 billion guilders of Dutch East Indies debt, a heavy burden for a new state.
West New Guinea was left to later negotiation, so the Dutch kept it and the question became a dispute with Indonesia.
A Netherlands-Indonesian Union was set up, but it was a weak link that did not last.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the proclamation (17 August 1945) with the transfer of sovereignty (27 December 1949). The Hague terms to know are the debt, West New Guinea and the Union.

notes.h: The Bandung Conference, 1955
notes.b: Even while Indonesia struggled at home, Sukarno gave it a voice abroad by hosting a conference of Asian and African states.
points: The Asian–African Conference at Bandung in April 1955 brought together 29 countries.
It promoted non-alignment (staying out of both Cold War blocs) and anti-colonialism (opposition to colonial rule).
Sukarno was its most prominent host, which raised his standing and Indonesia's among newly independent states.
notes.tip: Bandung is an achievement to cite: 29 countries, non-alignment and anti-colonialism, with Sukarno as host.

notes.h: Parliamentary democracy and regional rebellion, 1955–1958
notes.b: Independence did not bring stable government. Indonesia's parliamentary system produced weak governments, and the regions turned against Java.
points: The first free national election, in September 1955, left four parties of similar size (PNI, Masjumi, Nahdlatul Ulama and the PKI), so no party could govern alone and unstable coalition cabinets followed.
The regional rebellions of 1957–58, the PRRI in Sumatra and Permesta in Sulawesi, protested against Java's domination.
The army put the rebellions down, which strengthened the army's political role.

notes.h: Guided Democracy and Nasakom, 1959–1963
notes.b: Faced with instability, Sukarno ended parliamentary government and ruled through the army and a balance of political forces.
points: Sukarno introduced ‘Guided Democracy’ by decree on 5 July 1959, returning to the 1945 constitution and ruling with a National Front and the army. This ended parliamentary government.
He promoted ‘Nasakom’, from nasionalisme, agama (religion) and komunisme, the union of nationalism, religion and communism, so that all three groups would back his rule.
Sukarno had himself named president for life in 1963.
The PKI, with about three million members by the mid-1960s, was the largest communist party outside the communist states, and the army distrusted it.

notes.h: External problems: Dutch businesses and West New Guinea, 1957–1969
notes.b: Independence did not end the dispute with the Dutch. Sukarno turned on Dutch property and pressed Indonesia's claim to West New Guinea.
points: From 1957 Sukarno took over Dutch businesses in Indonesia, and the Dutch-owned enterprises were placed under Indonesian control.
West New Guinea stayed under Dutch rule until 1962, when it passed to a UN administration, and it was transferred to Indonesia on 1 May 1963.
A UN-supervised 1969 vote, the Act of Free Choice, confirmed Indonesian rule in West New Guinea. It was held among about 1,000 chosen representatives and has been widely criticised.

notes.h: Konfrontasi, the UN and China, 1963–1965
notes.b: In the early 1960s Sukarno turned Indonesia's energies outward, which isolated it abroad and drained its economy at home.
points: The Federation of Malaysia was formed in September 1963. Konfrontasi (confrontation), 1963–66, was Indonesia's opposition to it, including armed raids into Malaysian Borneo.
Sukarno withdrew Indonesia from the United Nations in January 1965 and moved towards closer relations with China.

notes.h: The crisis of 1965 and Sukarno's fall, 1965–1970
notes.b: Economic decline and the rivalry between the army and the PKI came to a head in 1965 and ended Sukarno's rule.
points: Economic decline in the early 1960s, with high inflation and heavy spending on Konfrontasi, weakened Sukarno's position, and the army grew more hostile to the PKI.
After an attempted coup on 30 September 1965 in which six generals were killed, General Suharto took control of the army.
Anti-communist killings followed, with estimates ranging from about 500,000 to 1 million or more.
The Supersemar order of 11 March 1966 stripped Sukarno of real power, and he was placed under house arrest.
Suharto became acting president in 1967 and president in 1968. Sukarno died in June 1970.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Sukarno with Suharto. Give dates for each stage: the coup attempt of 30 September 1965, the Supersemar order of 11 March 1966 and Suharto's presidency in 1968.

notes.h: Sukarno's Indonesia: internal and external problems
notes.b: Examiners often ask for the problems of Sukarno's Indonesia in two groups, internal and external. Each problem needs a named event with a date.
points: Internal problems: instability after the 1955 election, regional rebellion (PRRI and Permesta, 1957–58), the rivalry between the army and the PKI that led to the coup attempt of 30 September 1965, and economic decline in the early 1960s.

External problems: the Dutch and West New Guinea (Dutch rule to 1962, transfer in 1963), Konfrontasi against Malaysia (1963–66), and relations with the UN and China (Indonesia left the UN in January 1965).
notes.tip: For a question on the problems of Sukarno's Indonesia, sort your points into internal and external, and put a named event and a date on each.

notes.h: Key personality: Ho Chi Minh
notes.b: Ho Chi Minh led the Vietnamese independence movement from the 1920s and was the head of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. His career shows how a communist and nationalist leader used war and diplomacy to win independence.
points: Born Nguyen Sinh Cung in 1890 in central Vietnam, he left Vietnam in 1911 and spent about thirty years abroad, including in France, Britain, the Soviet Union and China. He used the name Nguyen Ai Quoc before adopting Ho Chi Minh in 1942.

Abroad, in 1919 he presented a petition for Vietnamese rights to the Versailles peace conference, which was ignored. He joined the French Communist Party in 1920, worked with the Communist International, and in 1930 helped found the Indochinese Communist Party.

He returned to Vietnam in 1941 and founded the Viet Minh, though the Chinese Nationalists held him in 1942–43. He was a participant in the August Revolution of 1945 and proclaimed the Democratic Republic on 2 September 1945.
As president of the Democratic Republic he led the war against France, with Vo Nguyen Giap commanding the army, so Ho provided political leadership while Giap led the fighting.

He was shaped by events as well as shaping them. The Japanese occupation broke French rule and the French attempt to return gave him the chance to lead a national movement, which he built on communist organisation.
Contemporaries in France and the United States regarded him as a communist agitator. Many Vietnamese nationalists regarded him as the leader who had made independence possible.
Historians debate whether his nationalism or his communism was the stronger force in his politics. They also debate the role of the Soviet Union and China in supporting him.

Known as ‘Uncle Ho’, he led North Vietnam after the 1954 division, where the Lao Dong Party ran the state with Soviet and Chinese aid. He died in September 1969, before the end of the Vietnam War, and Vietnam was unified under communist rule in 1975.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level profile of Ho, give dated points: birth, years abroad, the Communist Party, the Viet Minh in 1941, the proclamation on 2 September 1945, the war with France, Dien Bien Phu, Geneva and his death in 1969. Each correct, dated statement earns a mark.

notes.h: Key personality: Achmad Sukarno
notes.b: Sukarno was the first president of Indonesia and the central figure in the independence struggle against the Dutch. His career shows both what a gifted nationalist leader could achieve and where his methods failed.
points: Born on 6 June 1901 in East Java, he studied engineering at Bandung (graduating in 1926) and founded the Indonesian Nationalist Party (PNI) in 1927. The Dutch imprisoned him in 1929 and released him in 1931, then exiled him to remote islands until 1942.

Under the Japanese occupation he worked with the administration and encouraged mass mobilisation. Some Dutch and later Indonesian critics regarded this as collaboration, though it also gave him a mass audience.

On 1 June 1945 his Pancasila speech showed his aim of balancing nationalists, Muslims and communists in one state. He was a participant in the proclamation of 17 August 1945, with Hatta as vice-president, and became the first president.

He was a gifted orator who tried to hold together nationalists, religious groups, the army and the communists. He was never a leader of the PKI but worked closely with it in the early 1960s, which caused suspicion in the army.

His balance collapsed in 1965–66. After the coup attempt, Suharto took control of the army, the Supersemar order of 11 March 1966 stripped Sukarno of real power, and he was placed under house arrest until his death in June 1970.

Contemporaries were divided. Indonesians called him Bung Karno (brother Karno) and the father of the nation, while Dutch officials regarded him as a collaborator with Japan, and the army and the Islamic parties came to think him too close to the communists.

His later rule is judged harshly by many historians: Guided Democracy ended parliamentary government, and the economy and a foreign policy of confrontation left Indonesia isolated by 1965. Others credit him with giving a diverse archipelago a national language, Indonesian, and a unifying ideology in the Pancasila.
The historian Benedict Anderson, in Java in a Time of Revolution (1972), argued that the revolution was driven by young pemuda activists, trained under the Japanese, as much as by Sukarno and Hatta.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level profile of Sukarno, give dated points: birth in 1901, engineer, PNI in 1927, imprisonment in 1929, the Japanese occupation, the proclamation with Hatta, first president, Guided Democracy and his fall.

notes.h: Comparing the two struggles and the two leaders
notes.b: Ho Chi Minh and Sukarno both won independence, but they won it differently, and the European powers responded in different ways.
points: In Vietnam France fought a long war and was beaten at Dien Bien Phu, while in Indonesia the Dutch fought two police actions and then yielded to UN and US pressure.
Ho's method was armed struggle led by a communist party, and it produced a party-state in the North run by the Lao Dong Party.
Sukarno's method was negotiation, diplomacy and balancing, and in power it became a balancing act between nationalists, religious groups, the army and the communists, which collapsed in 1965.

Contemporary and later views differ for both men: Ho was a communist agitator to some and the leader of independence to others, while Sukarno was father of the nation to some and a collaborator or a failed ruler to others.
notes.tip: In comparison essays, contrast aims and methods (armed struggle and a communist party-state against negotiation, diplomacy and balancing), and how the colonial powers responded: France fought, while the Dutch fought and then yielded.

notes.h: Assessment: achievements and limits of the Indochinese and Indonesian independence movements
notes.b: Both movements won independence, but at a cost, and neither produced stable government. Weigh achievements against limits to reach a judgement.
points: Achievement: Vietnam and Indonesia both defeated attempts by returning colonial powers to restore their old authority, Indonesia in 1949 and the Viet Minh in 1954.
Achievement: Indonesia gained sovereignty in 1949 after a diplomatic campaign that involved the UN and the United States, not only military action.
Achievement: Sukarno's diplomacy at Bandung gave newly independent states a voice in world politics.
Limit: the Dutch police actions, the French war and the Geneva settlement all showed that European powers could resist independence for years.
Limit: Vietnam was divided in 1954, and the division became the basis of a larger war between the two Vietnamese states from the late 1950s.
Limit: Guided Democracy and the economic decline of the 1960s ended in the 1965 coup, the killings that followed, and Suharto's rise to power.
Limit: independence did not bring stable government, as Vietnam divided in 1954 and Indonesia moved from parliamentary democracy to authoritarian rule within a decade.
Later view: Benedict Anderson argued that the Indonesian revolution of 1945 was driven by young pemuda activists, trained under the Japanese, as much as by leaders such as Sukarno and Hatta.
notes.tip: In a Higher Level essay on Ho Chi Minh and Sukarno, state your judgement first, then set achievements (independence, defeat of colonial restoration) against limits (the division of Vietnam, authoritarian drift and 1965 in Indonesia), with dates.

keyTerms.definition: The control of a territory by an external power that governed it for the benefit of the imperial state.
The process by which colonies gained independence from their European rulers, most of it after 1945.
The federation set up by the French constitution of 1946, linking metropolitan France with its overseas territories and associated states.
The League for the Independence of Vietnam, founded in 1941 under Ho Chi Minh, which fought the French and the Japanese.
Sukarno's system from 1959, in which parliamentary democracy was replaced by presidential rule with the army and a National Front.
The Dutch term for their military operations in Indonesia in 1947 and 1948, which were not treated as a war.
Indonesia's campaign of opposition to the formation of Malaysia, from 1963 to 1966, including armed incursions into Borneo.
The five principles set out by Sukarno on 1 June 1945 as the basis of an independent Indonesian state.
Sukarno's formula for uniting nationalism (nasionalisme), religion (agama) and communism (komunisme) in his Guided Democracy.
The 1954 agreements that ended the First Indochina War, divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel and recognised the independence of Laos and Cambodia.
The April 1955 meeting of 29 Asian and African states in Indonesia that promoted non-alignment and anti-colonial co-operation.
The order of 11 March 1966 that gave General Suharto authority to restore order and in practice removed Sukarno's power.
